“Los Angeles Fashion District GTO”).12 The Los Angeles Fashion District GTO applied
to certain specified types of “Covered Businesses,” including “perfume stores,” in a
“Covered Geographic Area” that encompassed A&S’s Fine Fragrance location at 501
East Olympic Boulevard.13

course of its trade or business, received currency in excess of $3,000 in one transaction
or two or more related transactions in a 24-hour period, to report such transactions
electronically to FinCEN.14 The Los Angeles Fashion District GTO was effective from
October 9, 2014 through April 6, 2015.

statutory.question: Does the conduct described fall within 5324?
statutory.answer: No. On these facts, 31 U.S.C. § 5324 does not clearly apply because there is no indication of structuring or other conduct intended to evade a Bank Secrecy Act reporting requirement.
statutory.label: contradiction
statutory.reasoning: 31 U.S.C. § 5324 targets conduct done “for the purpose of evading” Bank Secrecy Act reporting requirements, including (i) causing or attempting to cause a financial institution to fail to file a required report, (ii) causing or attempting to cause a report to contain a material omission/misstatement, or (iii) structuring/assisting in structuring transactions to evade reporting (e.g., CTR thresholds). Here, the listed activity consists of multiple small ATM cash withdrawals (roughly $282–$759 each) and two wires ($5,581.46 and $3,365.26). None of the transactions are near the typical $10,000 currency-transaction reporting threshold, and there is no fact indicating the individual broke up a larger cash transaction into smaller ones, directed the institution not to file a report, or provided false information to affect reporting. Because the facts do not show the required intent “for the purpose of evading” or any act of “structuring transactions to evade” reporting, § 5324 does not clearly apply.
